content: 1. For adults, administer 3 grams of the combination of ampicillin (2 grams) and sulbactam (1 gram) intravenously every 6 hours, not exceeding a total daily dose of 12 grams. 2. For children and adolescents, the recommended dose is 100-200 mg of ampicillin per kilogram per day, divided into doses every 6 hours, administered intravenously. 3. For infants aged 1 month to 1 year, the dose is 100-150 mg of ampicillin per kilogram per day, divided into doses every 6 hours, administered intravenously or intramuscularly. 4. For children older than 1 year, the dose is 100-200 mg of ampicillin per kilogram per day, divided into doses every 6 hours, administered intravenously or intramuscularly. 5. For severe infections in infants aged 1 month to 1 year, the dose is increased to 200-300 mg of ampicillin per kilogram per day, divided into doses every 6 hours, administered intravenously or intramuscularly. 6. For severe infections in children older than 1 year, the dose is increased to 200-400 mg of ampicillin per kilogram per day, divided into doses every 6 hours, administered intravenously or intramuscularly. 7. Pain at the intramuscular injection site occurs in 16% of cases, diarrhea in 3%, pain at the intravenous injection site in 3%, and thrombophlebitis in 3%. Rash occurs in less than 2% of cases. 8. Other potential adverse effects include abdominal distension, black hairy tongue, candidiasis, chest pain, chills, dysuria, edema, epistaxis, erythema, fatigue, flatulence, glossitis, headache, itching, malaise, mucosal bleeding, nausea, pseudomembranous colitis, seizures, throat tightness, thrombocytopenia, urine retention, and vomiting. 9. Gastrointestinal disorders may include abdominal pain, cholestatic hepatitis, cholestasis, hyperbilirubinemia, jaundice, abnormal hepatic function, melena, gastritis, stomatitis, dyspepsia, and Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea. 10. Nervous system disorders may include convulsions and dizziness. 11. Respiratory, thoracic, and mediastinal disorders may include dyspnea. 12. Skin and subcutaneous tissue disorders may include toxic epidermal necrolysis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, angioedema, acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP), erythema multiforme, exfoliative dermatitis, urticaria, and linear IgA bullous dermatosis. 13. Immune disorders may include serious and potentially fatal hypersensitivity (anaphylactic) reactions. 14. Cardiac disorders may include acute myocardial ischemia, with or without myocardial infarction, as part of an allergic reaction. 15. Use caution in patients with hypersensitivity to the drug or its components, as well as in those with a history of cholestatic jaundice or hepatic dysfunction associated with ampicillin-sulbactam. 16. Exercise caution in patients with allergies to cephalosporins and carbapenems. 17. Adjust the dose in patients with renal failure. 18. Prolonged use is associated with fungal or bacterial superinfections. 19. Hepatic dysfunction, including hepatitis and cholestatic jaundice, has been reported. Hepatic toxicity is usually reversible, but fatalities have occurred. Monitor hepatic function regularly in patients with hepatic impairment. 20. A generalized dull red maculopapular rash may occur in 5-10% of children 3-14 days after initiating therapy. Carefully evaluate the rash to differentiate between a nonallergic ampicillin rash and a hypersensitivity reaction. The rash typically begins on the trunk and spreads over most of the body, with the most intense areas being pressure points, elbows, and knees. 21. Hepatotoxicity has been reported; monitor hepatic function regularly in patients with hepatic impairment. 22. A high percentage of patients with infectious mononucleosis develop a rash during therapy; therapy is not recommended in these patients. 23. Severe skin reactions, such as toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS), exfoliative dermatitis, erythema multiforme, and acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP), may occur. If a skin rash develops, monitor closely and discontinue therapy if lesions progress. 24. Pregnancy category B: Generally acceptable. Controlled studies in pregnant women show no evidence of fetal risk. 25. Lactation: The drug is excreted in breast milk; use with caution. 26. This drug is a combination of a beta-lactamase inhibitor with ampicillin. It interferes with bacterial cell wall synthesis during active replication, resulting in bactericidal activity against susceptible organisms. It serves as an alternative to amoxicillin when oral administration is not possible and provides coverage for skin, enteric flora, and anaerobes. It is not ideal for nosocomial pathogens. 27. Additive effects may occur with aminoglycosides and ciprofloxacin. 28. For intramuscular (IM) administration, reconstitute with 2% or 5% lidocaine injection to obtain a 250 mg ampicillin-125 mg sulbactam/mL solution. Use within 1 hour after preparation. 29. For intravenous (IV) administration, further dilute to 3-45 mg/mL with an appropriate diluent. Use normal saline (NS) for IV piggyback. Use within 8 hours after preparation. 30. Administer the drug around the clock to minimize variations in peak and trough serum levels. 31. Administer IV injections slowly over at least 10-15 minutes or as an infusion over 15-30 minutes. 32. For IM administration, inject deeply into a large muscle mass. 33. Store intact vials at temperatures below 30°C. 34.
